decisions.mark: states that by default the macro RENAMES the member to private_<member>, and that defining MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS makes it expand to the member name unchanged
decisions.detail: QUOTE: By default it expands to `private_##m`, so the member is declared as `private_m` in the public header. ... Inside those translation units `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(m)` becomes plain `m` | WHY: The answer states the default expansion to `private_m` and that the macro becomes plain `m` where `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` is defined (it names that macro as the opt-out, defined in `common.h` and the example programs).

decisions.mark: explains that the two branches give different consumers different views — code that defines MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS sees plain member names while an ordinary consumer of the public headers sees the renamed ones
decisions.detail: QUOTE: Inside those translation units `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(m)` becomes plain `m`, so the code can write `ctx->grp.id` directly ... and "By default it expands to `private_##m`, so the member is declared as `private_m` in the public header. The effect is that plain `ctx->m` fails to compile for anyone outside the library." | WHY: The answer states that where the opt-out is defined the names are plain, while ordinary consumers of the public headers see `private_`-renamed members and must use the explicit spelling.

decisions.mark: concludes that this enforces API opacity at COMPILE time by breaking the member name, rather than by hiding the struct layout — the fields remain visible and sized
decisions.detail: QUOTE: The effect is that plain `ctx->m` fails to compile for anyone outside the library. The name is the only thing that changes. The layout does not, so the mangling is not an ABI change. | WHY: The answer says the compile-time barrier comes from renaming the member (`private_m`) while the layout stays unchanged, so the fields remain visible.
